event.title: Deep Matters 2026
event.about: The Deep Matters conference series is back! This year, we explore how AI agents are transforming the way science is done — from hypothesis generation to decision making to knowledge discovery. Don't miss this one-day event for everyone across academia, industry and startups.
event.registerNote: Free · Limited places, subject to approval.

venue.name: Institute of Physics
venue.directions: 5 mins walk from King's Cross St Pancras

sheares-toh.name: Sheares Toh
sheares-toh.bio: Sheares builds AI agents for scientific discovery and optimisation in self-driving labs. He is also an avid chess player and a watch aficionado.

sam-cooper.name: Prof Sam Cooper
sam-cooper.role: Professor in AI for Materials Design
sam-cooper.bio: Sam leads the Tools for Learning, Design and Research (TLDR) group in the Dyson School of Design Engineering. He is also co-founder and Chief Scientist at Polaron.

davide-tisi.name: Dr Davide Tisi
davide-tisi.bio: Davide is a postdoc in the Autonomous Materials Discovery group at DTU Energy. He uses machine-learning potentials to study materials for energy storage.

pascal-friederich.name: Prof Pascal Friederich
pascal-friederich.role: Professor in AI for Materials Science
pascal-friederich.bio: Pascal leads the AI for Materials Science (AiMat) group at KIT, developing machine learning methods for property prediction, simulation, understanding, and design of molecules and materials.

abdoulatif-cisse.name: Dr Abdoulatif Cissé
abdoulatif-cisse.bio: Abdoulatif Cissé is a postdoc in the Cooper Group at the University of Liverpool, where he works on bringing chemical reasoning to mobile robot chemists and exploring how researchers and robots can work together.

yue-wu.name: Dr Yue Wu
yue-wu.bio: Yue is CSO of Lightning Tree, a battery startup in Cambridge. He also develops rietx, an open-source Rietveld package built for AI agents as a way to democratise scientific expertise.

items.title: AI for Materials Science: From Autonomous Materials Optimisation to the Generation of Novel Ideas
items.abstract: AI and machine learning methods are playing an increasingly important role in materials science and chemistry. They can accelerate the screening, design, and discovery of new molecules and materials in multiple ways, e.g. by virtually predicting properties of molecules and materials, by extracting hidden relations from large amounts of simulated or experimental data, or even by interfacing machine learning algorithms for autonomous decision-making directly with automated experiments. In this talk, I will focus on our research activities on automated data analysis and autonomous decision-making in self-driving labs ([Wu et al., Science, 2024](https://www.science.org/doi/abs/10.1126/science.ads0901)), as well as our work on predicting new research directions in materials science using large language models and concept graphs ([Marwitz et al., Nature Machine Intelligence, 2026](https://doi.org/10.1038/s42256-026-01206-y)).

items.title: MAESTRO: Knowing the What, When and Where in Experimental Optimisation
From Bayesian Optimisation to AI Agents: Lessons from a Robotic Chemistry Lab
items.abstract: Bayesian optimisation can guide searches through complex experimental spaces, while large language models contribute scientific context and generate hypotheses. This talk traces the progression from BORA, a hybrid Bayesian optimisation framework, to LLM agents guiding experiments in a closed-loop robotic chemistry laboratory. In a noisy, 25-variable photocatalytic hydrogen-production study, an agent's recommendations were benchmarked against human domain experts. The comparison highlights a trade-off: experts found a more active catalyst formulation, while the agent reasoned much faster and at far lower cost.

items.title: rietx: Scientific Software for Agents, by Agents
items.abstract: In this talk, I describe how we use agentic software engineering to rapidly develop rietx: a new Rietveld refinement package designed from the ground up to enable agentic operation with cheap, easily accessible models. Rietveld refinement of powder diffraction data is commonly considered one of the gold standards for structural characterization. As such, it’s a key part of any self-driving lab workflow for materials discovery. Many efforts have focused on training predictive models or wrapping legacy Rietveld refinement packages as tools for AI agents. With rietx, we invert the problem by creating a tool agents can use easily. I’ll show some demonstrations of autonomous refinement, discuss our development model and present some use cases rietx has found in the materials science community.
